title: Antony's Funeral Speech
text:
After Caesar was assassinated, Brutus spoke first to the Roman crowd. He explained that he had loved Caesar, but loved Rome more, and had killed him because he was ambitious. The crowd cheered Brutus. He then allowed Mark Antony to speak at the funeral, on condition that Antony not blame the conspirators.

Antony began by agreeing. He had come, he said, to bury Caesar, not to praise him. Brutus said Caesar was ambitious, and Brutus was an honorable man. Then he reminded them of things they knew: Caesar had filled Rome's treasury with ransoms, had wept when the poor cried, and had three times refused a crown. Each time, he repeated that Brutus was an honorable man, until the words began to sound like an accusation.

He mentioned Caesar's will, then said he should not read it, because it would inflame them. The crowd demanded it. Instead he came down among them, held up Caesar's bloodied cloak, and showed them the tears made by each dagger, including the one by Brutus, whom Caesar had loved. Then he uncovered the body.

Only then did he read the will, which left money to every citizen and Caesar's gardens to the public. The crowd broke into a riot, set out to burn the conspirators' houses, and Brutus and Cassius fled the city.
lesson: People are moved more by what they work out for themselves than by what they are told. Concede the surface, then let facts and curiosity carry them to your conclusion.
people: Mark Antony, Brutus, the Roman crowd
source: William Shakespeare, Julius Caesar, Act 3, Scene 2
